n: Interpretation of Abnormal Liver Function Tests

faq.a: No; early viral hepatitis may have normal ALT, so consider exposure history and repeat testing if suspicion remains.
faq.q: Can a normal ALT rule out hepatitis?

faq.a: GGT helps confirm that an elevated ALP is of hepatic origin rather than bone.
faq.q: Why is GGT measured with ALP?

faq.a: Rely on the biochemical pattern (ALP/GGT ↑) and clinical signs (jaundice, RUQ tenderness) to infer obstruction.

exam: A 28‑year‑old with fever, right‑upper‑quadrant pain and ALT 600 U/L – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Consider acute malaria or viral hepatitis; obtain malaria test, start ACT if positive, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
Patient on TB therapy presents with ALT 450 U/L (5 × ULN) but is asymptomatic – what do you do? — Stop isoniazid/pyrazinamide, switch to levofloxacin‑based regimen, monitor LFTs.
Child with sickle‑cell disease has bilirubin 12 mg/dL, normal ALP – what is the cause? — Hemolytic jaundice; treat underlying sickle crisis, no need for biliary imaging.
How does cholestatic pattern differ from hepatocellular on LFTs? — ALP and GGT dominate in cholestasis; ALT/AST dominate in hepatocellular injury.
Why avoid NSAIDs in a patient with INR 1.8? — NSAIDs increase bleeding risk when synthetic function is impaired.
What red‑flag on LFTs mandates urgent referral? — INR >1.5, bilirubin >10 mg/dL, or encephalopathy.
Explain why albumin may be normal in acute liver failure. — Albumin has a long half‑life; it falls only after weeks of synthetic loss.
In a malaria‑endemic area, which test is most useful when LFTs are abnormal and fever is present? — Rapid malaria test or thick smear; positive result directs antimalarial therapy.
ai.title: Interpretation of Abnormal Liver Function Tests
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A systematic approach to abnormal LFTs helps identify the site of liver injury, common tropical causes, and urgent threats. Use patterns, clinical clues and limited investigations to guide management in low‑resource settings.

b: ALT/AST – hepatocellular injury
ALP/GGT – cholestasis
Bilirubin – excretory function
Albumin/INR – synthetic function
sections.p: Liver function tests (LFTs) are a group of serum enzymes and proteins that reflect hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, or synthetic failure. In low‑resource hospitals the panel often includes ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.

b: Isolated ALT/AST ↑ → viral hepatitis, drug/toxin, malaria, sickle‑cell crisis
Predominant ALP ↑ with ↑ GGT → biliary obstruction, cholangitis, schistosomiasis
High bilirubin with normal enzymes → hemolysis or Gilbert’s
Low albumin or prolonged INR → chronic liver disease, malnutrition
sections.p: Interpretation starts with the pattern (which tests are raised) and magnitude (how many times upper limit). Then consider clinical context, risk factors and endemic diseases.

b: Identify patients needing urgent referral (e.g., INR >1.5, bilirubin >10 mg/dL)
Guide choice of anti‑infective therapy (avoid hepatotoxic drugs if ALT >5 × ULN)
Monitor drug toxicity in HIV/TB co‑treated patients
sections.p: Abnormal LFTs may be the first clue to life‑threatening conditions such as acute viral hepatitis, sepsis‑related cholestasis, or hepatic failure from malaria or TB drugs.

t.b: Is the injury hepatocellular? – >5 × ULN suggests acute hepatitis; >10 × ULN raises concern for ischemic injury or toxin
Is cholestasis present? – ALP >2 × ULN with GGT ↑ points to biliary obstruction or infiltrative disease
Is excretory function impaired? – Direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL with ALP ↑ suggests obstructive jaundice
Is synthetic function failing? – Albumin <3 g/dL or INR >1.5 indicates decompensated chronic disease

t.a: Hepatitis serology (HBsAg, anti‑HBc IgM, HCV Ab)
t.b: Is viral hepatitis the cause? – Positive result confirms acute or chronic infection

t.a: Malaria rapid test or thick smear
t.b: Is malaria causing hepatic injury? – Positive in febrile patients with high transaminases
Is there biliary dilatation or focal lesion? – Dilated ducts confirm obstruction; absent if not available, rely on ALP/GGT pattern

b: Acute viral hepatitis – supportive care, avoid hepatotoxic drugs, give vitamin K if INR >1.5
Malaria‑related hepatitis – give ACT (artemisinin‑based combination therapy) promptly
TB drug‑induced injury – stop isoniazid/pyrazinamide if ALT >5 × ULN, switch to non‑hepatotoxic regimen
Obstructive jaundice – refer for drainage; give broad‑spectrum antibiotics if cholangitis suspected
Chronic liver disease – nutritional support, treat hepatitis B with tenofovir (if available), vaccinate against hepatitis A
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; support hepatic function and monitor for deterioration.

b: Hemolysis – ↑ indirect bilirubin, normal ALT/AST
Muscle injury – ↑ AST > ALT, CK markedly raised
Pregnancy cholestasis – ↑ ALP (bone isoenzyme), pruritus, normal ALT
sections.p: Conditions that raise similar labs but have different pathophysiology.

b: Late‑stage cirrhosis may show normal ALT despite severe disease
GGT can be normal in early biliary obstruction
Albumin falls slowly; acute liver failure may have normal albumin
sections.p: Certain factors blunt or exaggerate LFT values.

b: ALT >5 × ULN + recent fever → think malaria or viral hepatitis
ALP >2 × ULN + right‑upper‑quadrant pain → obstructive cause
INR >1.5 in any setting → consider transfer to higher‑level care
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, common tropical etiologies, and urgent red‑flags.

whenToSeekHelp: INR >1.5 or rapidly rising bilirubin >10 mg/dL
Severe abdominal pain with fever and jaundice (possible cholangitis)
